prompt: A pull request renames module.database.primary to module.data.primary. The plan proposes creating a new database and deleting the old database, while the author says this is only a code refactor. Diagnose the risk and describe the safe evidence path.
directAnswer: The configuration address is part of the tool's ownership identity. Without a supported moved/refactor declaration or a carefully reviewed state operation, the old address appears removed and the new address appears added, so create/delete is expected. Stop before apply, map both addresses to the exact remote database ID and state lineage, confirm the intended object is unchanged, use the product's supported identity-preserving mechanism, regenerate a full plan and require zero replacement. Protect data with tested backup/restore and verify dependants even after an identity-preserving plan.
foundation: Configuration, state and remote reality are different. State binds one configuration address to one remote object. A source rename changes the address even when business intent has not changed. A syntactically valid plan is still dangerous if ownership moved incorrectly. Identity changes require explicit evidence and review.
reasoningSteps: Record source revision, tool/provider/module versions, target, backend, workspace, state lineage and serial.
Read the full replacement reason rather than aggregate action counts.
Map old configuration address to its current remote database ID.
Confirm the new address is intended to own that same single remote object.
Check whether the tool/version supports a declarative moved or refactor construct for this address change.
If a state operation is necessary, take a protected snapshot and use the supported command under peer review; do not edit JSON manually.
Regenerate a complete refreshed plan and require the database action to become no-op or an understood in-place change.
Review downstream references, outputs, policies and module consumers for address or contract changes.
Confirm backup and restore evidence because accidental replacement remains a high-consequence failure mode.
After authorized execution, verify state binding, remote ID, data, connectivity, user SLI and a fresh full no-change plan.
seniorAnswer: I would reject the claim that this is only a text refactor. In stateful IaC, the resource address is the ownership key. I would freeze execution and compare the old binding, new desired address, remote database ID, state lineage/serial and plan replacement reason. If logical ownership is unchanged, I would use the version-supported moved/refactor mechanism; a direct state move is a governed fallback with snapshot, exact addresses, peer review and recovery. The replacement must disappear from a newly generated full plan bound to the current state. Because the object is stateful, I would still require tested backup/restore, dependent-service checks, a rollback or roll-forward decision and post-change verification. I would never approve delete/create merely because the source diff is small.
weakAnswer: Apply the plan because Terraform will recreate the same database, then restore the data if needed.
whyWeak: It accepts unnecessary destructive replacement, assumes identity and data can be recreated, ignores state bindings and supported refactor mechanisms, and has no target, backup, dependency, approval or verification evidence.

evidence.signal: Plan shows delete old address and create new address
evidence.proves: For the exact plan inputs, the engine interprets two ownership lifecycles.
evidence.doesNotProve: That replacement is desired, safe or actually executed.

evidence.signal: Old state binding points to remote ID db-4402
evidence.proves: That state snapshot maps the old address to that ID.
evidence.doesNotProve: Current remote health, data correctness or exclusive ownership.

evidence.signal: New plan after moved declaration shows no replacement
evidence.proves: The selected tool/version preserves the binding in that proposal.
evidence.doesNotProve: Application compatibility, data integrity or post-apply health.

followUps.prompt: Why not edit the state JSON?
followUps.answer: The format can change and manual editing bypasses validation, lineage and supported identity operations. Use product commands or declarative refactors with snapshots and review.

followUps.prompt: Does prevent-destroy make the rename safe?
followUps.answer: It may block one deletion path, but it does not repair ownership, prevent duplicate creation or protect changes outside that configuration.
A resource address is ownership identity; preserve the binding before treating a rename as refactor.

rubric.observableEvidence: Explains address-to-remote binding and why rename appears destructive.
Captures source, target, tool/provider and state lineage/serial.
Uses supported moved/refactor or governed state operation and a fresh plan.
Requires backup/restore and downstream compatibility evidence.
Checks binding, remote ID, data, users and a full no-change plan.
